0.title: When God Speaks Through a Sermon
0.essay:
Every Sunday, in thousands of churches, someone stands up, opens a Bible and speaks for half an hour or so. To an outsider it can look like an odd survival from another age: a lecture without slides, a speech without applause. Yet Christians have always believed that something far greater happens there. When the Bible is faithfully preached, God himself speaks.

Why this study

This study is for preachers, for the elders who oversee them, and just as much for ordinary church members. Most Christians will never preach a sermon, but every Christian hears hundreds of them. We need to know what good preaching is, so that we can recognise it, receive it, pray for it and gently encourage it. Paul told the Thessalonians that they had received his preaching “not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, which is at work in you believers” (1 Thessalonians 2:13). That is a remarkable claim, and it shapes everything that follows.

Principles and practice

We begin with principles: what preaching is, why God has chosen it, what it means to preach the point of a passage, and how every part of Scripture leads us to Christ. Then we turn to the preacher himself, and to the practical work of speaking to real hearts with clarity and warmth. We end with the week of preparation behind a sermon, and with the hearer’s side: how to listen well, and how to test and encourage preaching kindly.

This study builds on Hermeneutics, which explains how to read the Bible carefully, and sits beside Worship & the Lord’s Day, The Church and Christ in the Old Testament.

The chapters

What Preaching Is and Why God Uses It; Preaching the Point of the Passage; Preaching Christ from All the Scriptures; The Preacher’s Life and Prayer; Reaching the Heart; and Preparing, Hearing and Encouraging Sermons. One question is handled with the main views and this commentary’s view: who may preach in the gathered church.

For reflection

What do you usually expect to happen when you sit under a sermon? Can you remember a sermon God used to change you, and why did it reach you?

1.title: What Preaching Is and Why God Uses It
1.essay:
Preaching is the public proclamation of God’s word by someone sent to do it, explaining what the Bible says and pressing it on the hearers so that they believe and obey. It is more than a talk about religion. It is a herald announcing news from the King, and calling people to respond.

Heralds, not lecturers

The New Testament uses several words for this work. One means to proclaim as a herald. Another means to announce good news. Others mean to teach, to reason, to exhort and to testify. A herald does not make up the message; he delivers it. That is why Paul says, “For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake” (2 Corinthians 4:5). The preacher’s authority is borrowed. He has authority only so far as he says what God has said.

So preaching is both teaching and appeal. It explains, and it pleads. “We are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20). A sermon that only informs has not yet finished its work.

How faith comes

Why does God use preaching at all? Paul gives a chain of reasoning: “How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent?” (Romans 10:14–15). Then he concludes: “So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17).

Notice the last phrase. Through the preacher’s voice, people hear Christ himself. Jesus said to those he sent, “The one who hears you hears me” (Luke 10:16). This is why the Reformers spoke so boldly. Heinrich Bullinger’s Second Helvetic Confession of 1566 says, “The preaching of the Word of God is the Word of God.” The confession immediately makes clear that this is true when the preacher faithfully proclaims Scripture, and that the word does not depend on the preacher’s own worth. A weak and sinful man may hold a treasure that is not his.

The Westminster Larger Catechism (Question 155) says that the Spirit of God makes the reading, but especially the preaching, of the word an effectual means of enlightening, convincing and humbling sinners, of driving them out of themselves and drawing them to Christ, and of building believers up in grace and comfort. Preaching is one of God’s chief means of grace, not a human performance.

The folly of preaching

God could have chosen many other ways. He chose this one, and he chose it partly because it looks weak. “For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe” (1 Corinthians 1:21). Paul came to Corinth, a city that loved polished speakers, and refused to compete with them: “my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:4–5).

The power is not in technique. It is in God’s word, carried by God’s Spirit. “Is not my word like fire, declares the LORD, and like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces?” (Jeremiah 23:29). And it never fails in what God intends: “it shall not return to me empty” (Isaiah 55:11).

Giving the sense

One of the earliest pictures of preaching comes after the exile. The people gathered in Jerusalem, Ezra read the Law from a wooden platform, and the Levites helped them understand. “They read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading” (Nehemiah 8:8). Reading, explaining, understanding: that is the heart of preaching. And the people wept, then rejoiced, because they had understood. Nehemiah told them, “the joy of the LORD is your strength” (Nehemiah 8:10).

Preach the word

Paul’s last letter gives Timothy a solemn charge, made “in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead” (2 Timothy 4:1). What is the charge? “preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort, with complete patience and teaching” (2 Timothy 4:2). He adds a warning that sounds very modern: “people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions” (2 Timothy 4:3). The preacher is not there to scratch itches but to feed souls.

A woman came to church most Sundays out of habit, tired from a hard week. She thought of the sermon as a talk to be politely endured. One morning the preacher opened Isaiah 40 and explained, carefully and warmly, why God’s people could take comfort. Nothing about the delivery was dramatic. But she went home knowing that God had spoken to her. From then on she came expecting to hear him.

The God who speaks

Behind all this lies the wonder of a God who speaks. He spoke the world into being. “Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:1–2). He still speaks that finished word by his Spirit, through ordinary people with Bibles open. Preaching is one of the ways the living God keeps his promise not to leave his people alone.

For reflection

How would you explain the difference between a lecture and a sermon? What does Romans 10:14–17 teach about why preaching matters? Do you come to church expecting God to speak? How might that expectation change the way you listen?

2.title: Preaching the Point of the Passage
2.essay:
The simplest description of good preaching is this: the point of the passage is the point of the sermon. Expository preaching is not one style among many. It is the conviction that the preacher’s message should come out of the text, rather than being brought to it.

What expository means

To expound is to lay open. An expository sermon explains what a passage of Scripture says and means, and then applies that meaning to the hearers. Some sermons cover a few verses, others a whole chapter or even a whole book. Some follow the order of a book week by week; others gather several passages on a theme. The length and plan can vary. What matters is that the message of the sermon is the message of the text, so that the congregation leaves having heard what God said, not merely what the preacher thinks.

The opposite is the “springboard” sermon. The preacher reads a verse, then jumps off it into whatever he wanted to say. The verse becomes a decoration. Over time, a church fed on springboard sermons hears only the preacher’s favourite ideas and never learns to read the Bible for itself.

Rightly handling the word

Paul told Timothy, “Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2:15). The picture is of a workman cutting straight. Handling the word rightly takes effort. Ezra is the model: “For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel” (Ezra 7:10). Study, then obedience, then teaching. The order matters.

Careful handling means asking the questions explained in the study Hermeneutics. What did this mean to its first readers? What kind of writing is it: narrative, law, poetry, prophecy, letter, apocalyptic? What comes before and after? How does it fit the book’s purpose and the Bible’s whole story? A psalm of lament must not be preached like a page of Romans, and a story about David must not be turned into a set of rules. The genre shapes the sermon.

Why it matters

Expository preaching guards the church in several ways. It keeps the preacher under God’s authority, because the text sets the agenda. It protects the congregation from the preacher’s hobby horses, because the passage in front of him forces him to say things he might not have chosen. It teaches people how to read their Bibles, because they watch it being done week by week. And it gives “the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20:27), the hard parts as well as the comfortable ones.

It also gives the preacher courage. When he must say something unwelcome, he can point to the text and say, in effect, “This is not my idea. Look, it is here.” The hearers can check, and they should.

One main point

Most passages have a main thrust. A sermon is clearest when it finds that thrust and lets every part serve it. The preacher should be able to state, in one sentence, what the passage is saying, and then, in another, what it is saying to us. If he cannot, he is not yet ready to preach it. Many details in a passage are interesting, but a sermon is not a commentary. Faithful preachers leave out much that they have learned, so that the one thing the text is saying comes through clearly.

Exposition is not dryness

Some fear that expository preaching means a dull, verse-by-verse lecture full of Greek words. It need not. Jesus’ hearers “were astonished at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes” (Matthew 7:28–29). The scribes quoted authorities; Jesus spoke with the authority of God. A preacher who has wrestled with the text until he sees what it says will speak with a quiet authority that does not come from personality. The text itself is alive: “the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword” (Hebrews 4:12). Exposition lets the sword cut.

A young preacher learns

A young man in his first pastorate used to choose a topic on Monday, then search for a verse to hang it on. His sermons were lively, but his people knew little of their Bibles. An older minister suggested he preach through Mark’s Gospel, letting each passage decide the subject. At first he found it frightening. Some weeks the text said things he would never have chosen. But his people began to bring their Bibles, to ask questions about the passage, and to read Mark at home. He discovered that the Bible was a far better preacher than he was.

Topical and doctrinal sermons

Is there no place for a sermon on a topic, such as marriage or the Trinity or grief? There is. Paul’s letters often gather teaching on a theme. But a good topical sermon is still expository in spirit: it takes its main points from passages rightly understood in context, and does not use verses as proof texts torn from their setting. The test is always the same: is the authority in the sermon the authority of the text?

For reflection

Can you remember a sermon where the text was only a springboard? How did it differ from one where the passage set the agenda? Why does it help a church to hear books of the Bible preached in order? Try summarising last Sunday’s passage in one sentence.

3.title: Preaching Christ from All the Scriptures
3.essay:
On the evening of the first Easter Sunday, the risen Jesus walked with two discouraged disciples and gave them the most wonderful Bible study ever taught: “And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). Every faithful sermon follows where he led.

The whole Bible is about him

Jesus said of the Old Testament, “it is they that bear witness about me” (John 5:39). Later that same Easter evening he told the eleven that “everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44). Then he summed up the message of the Scriptures: “that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead, and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations” (Luke 24:46–47).

So Christian preaching is Christ-centred, not because the preacher forces Jesus into every text, but because the Bible itself is one story with Christ at its centre. Paul could sum up his whole ministry in one sentence: “For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2). That did not mean Paul never spoke about money, marriage or church order. It meant that he spoke of everything in the light of the cross.

The apostles show us how

The sermons in Acts are our best models. Peter at Pentecost explains Joel and the Psalms, then drives home the point: “God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts 2:36). The hearers “were cut to the heart” (Acts 2:37). In Thessalonica Paul “reasoned with them from the Scriptures, explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead” (Acts 17:2–3). In Pisidian Antioch he traced Israel’s history to David and from David to Jesus, and concluded, “through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you” (Acts 13:38). The apostles read the Old Testament as a story heading somewhere, and they showed their hearers where.

Roads to Christ, not tricks

How does a preacher get from an Old Testament passage to Christ honestly? Not by allegory, where every detail becomes a hidden symbol (the scarlet cord of Rahab as the blood of Christ, the five smooth stones as five wounds). That makes the Bible a code, and it teaches people that only clever preachers can understand it. The study Christ in the Old Testament and the study Hermeneutics set out the sound paths. Briefly:

There are promises that Christ fulfils, from the offspring of the woman in Genesis 3 to the Servant of Isaiah 53. There are patterns or types, real people and institutions that foreshadow him: the Passover lamb, the priesthood, the temple, David the king. There are themes running through the whole Bible, such as sacrifice, exile and return, the shepherd, the kingdom, that come to rest in him. There is contrast: Adam fails where Christ obeys, and Israel grumbles in the wilderness where Jesus trusts his Father. And there is the need that every passage exposes, which only the gospel meets. The Old Testament law shows God’s holiness and our failure, and so it sends us to the One who kept it for us.

The preacher should first preach what the text says in its own setting. The road to Christ then runs through the passage’s main point, not around it.

The danger of moralism

The opposite mistake is moralism: turning the Bible into a book of good examples and good advice. David and Goliath becomes “face your giants with courage”. Joseph becomes “stay pure and you will be promoted”. These sermons are not entirely wrong; the Bible does give examples (1 Corinthians 10:6). But if that is all we say, we have preached a religion of self-improvement, and we have quietly told people they can save themselves.

Timothy Keller often pointed out that there are two ways to miss the gospel: by irreligion, which ignores God’s law, and by religion, which tries to keep it in order to earn God’s favour. Moralistic preaching breeds the second. It produces either proud people who think they are doing well, or crushed people who know they are not. Keller urged preachers to show that the Bible is not mainly about us and what we must do, but about God and what he has done in Christ. David is not first our example; he is the anointed king who fights the enemy his people cannot face, and so points to the greater Son of David who won the decisive battle for us.

From Christ to obedience

Christ-centred preaching is not soft on obedience. It grounds obedience in grace. “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives” (Titus 2:11–12). Grace trains. When people see what Christ has done, they want to obey, and they find strength to begin.

A preacher once preached the Joseph story as a lesson in resisting temptation. Years later he preached it again, and this time he showed the brothers bowing before the one they had betrayed, and Joseph weeping and forgiving them. He pointed to the greater Brother, rejected by his own, who became the means of their rescue. A man who had heard both sermons told him afterwards that the first had made him feel guilty; the second had made him want to be like Joseph, because he had seen Jesus.

The Puritan William Perkins ended his manual on preaching with a sentence every preacher could pin above his desk: “Preach one Christ by Christ to the praise of Christ.”

For reflection

Why is allegory an unsafe road to Christ? What would a moralistic sermon on your favourite Bible story sound like, and how would a Christ-centred one differ? How does seeing Christ’s work change your motive for obedience? Read Luke 24:13–35 and notice what made the disciples’ hearts burn.

4.title: The Preacher’s Life and Prayer
4.essay:
God does not send sermons by post. He sends them through people, and the person matters. Paul told Timothy, “Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers” (1 Timothy 4:16). The preacher’s life and his doctrine go together.

Watch your life

The qualifications for elders in 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 are mostly about character. Only one, “able to teach” (1 Timothy 3:2), concerns gifts. The rest concern self-control, gentleness, faithfulness in marriage, honesty with money, a well-ordered home and a good reputation. A brilliant speaker who is harsh at home or careless with the truth will undo with his life what he says with his lips. Hearers notice. “Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God. Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith” (Hebrews 13:7).

The preacher must first preach to himself. Before he asks others to repent, he must repent. Before he offers Christ to others, he must feed on Christ himself. Richard Baxter, the Puritan pastor of Kidderminster, wrote that he preached as never sure to preach again, “as a dying man to dying men.” That kind of seriousness grows only in a man who has felt the weight of eternity in his own soul.

Prayer and the word

When the early church faced a practical crisis, the apostles appointed others to serve, saying, “But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word” (Acts 6:4). Notice which comes first. Preaching without prayer is speaking to people about God without first speaking to God about people. The preacher prays as he studies: “Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). He prays for his hearers by name. He prays before he stands up, knowing that only the Spirit can give life: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all” (John 6:63).

This is the great relief of preaching. “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). The preacher cannot open one heart. He can be faithful, and leave the fruit to God.

The church prays too

Paul, apostle and missionary, repeatedly asked ordinary Christians to pray for his preaching: “pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ … that I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak” (Colossians 4:3–4). He asked the Ephesians to pray “that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel” (Ephesians 6:19). Clarity and boldness: those are two things every congregation can ask God to give its preachers.

A pastor in a small church had grown weary. Saturday nights were spent anxiously polishing, and Sunday mornings felt like an exam. An elder noticed, and quietly began meeting with two others early on Sunday mornings to pray for him and for the hearers. The pastor did not change his method. But he began to preach with a new freedom, knowing he was carried by his people’s prayers. Over time others joined that prayer meeting, and the whole church began to listen differently.

Weakness and dependence

Preachers are not supermen. “But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us” (2 Corinthians 4:7). Many faithful ministers struggle with discouragement, criticism, loneliness and exhaustion. Some battle depression. A pastor who is sinking should talk to a trusted fellow elder, rest, and see a doctor; medicine and counselling are no failure of faith (see the study Depression & the Christian). If thoughts of ending his life come, he must seek help at once: emergency services, a crisis line, a trusted person. Churches should give their pastors real rest and care, not only demands.

Who may preach?

Scripture calls those who preach in the gathered church to be gifted, tested and recognised. James wrote, “Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness” (James 3:1). A man may desire the work, but the church must recognise that God has given him the gifts and character for it (1 Timothy 3:1–7; 2 Timothy 2:2).

Christians differ on whether women may preach in the gathered church. Egalitarians, many of them deeply committed to Scripture, point to women who prophesied (Acts 2:17; 1 Corinthians 11:5), to Priscilla explaining the way of God to Apollos (Acts 18:26), to Phoebe and Junia (Romans 16), and to the unity of men and women in Christ (Galatians 3:28). They read 1 Timothy 2:12 as a word for a particular situation in Ephesus. Complementarians agree that women and men are equal in dignity and gifts, and that women teach in many settings. But they hold that Paul’s words, “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man” (1 Timothy 2:12), are grounded in creation (1 Timothy 2:13), not local custom, and refer to the authoritative teaching of the gathered church that belongs to the elders.

This commentary’s view: the eldership and the authoritative preaching of the gathered church belong to qualified men, grounded in creation order. This is not a judgment on women’s gifts. Women have taught, prophesied and served richly throughout Scripture and church history, and many have taught preachers a great deal, as Priscilla did. Everything in this study about hearing, testing and praying for sermons belongs to every member, men and women alike.

For reflection

Why does a preacher’s life matter as much as his words? What would it look like for you to pray regularly for those who preach to you, and what would you ask for? How can your church care for its pastors? Read 1 Timothy 4:12–16 and note what Paul asks of a young preacher.

5.title: Reaching the Heart
5.essay:
A sermon can be true in every sentence and still never land. Good preaching explains the text, and then carries its truth to the heart, so that people are moved to believe, repent, love and obey. The Westminster Larger Catechism (Question 159) asks ministers to preach plainly, faithfully, wisely and zealously, “applying themselves to the necessities and capacities of the hearers.”

Truth that reaches the heart

In the Bible the heart is not merely the feelings. It is the control centre of the person: what we love, trust and want. Sermons must engage the mind, but they aim through the mind at the heart. When Peter preached at Pentecost, his hearers “were cut to the heart” (Acts 2:37). When the risen Jesus opened the Scriptures, the disciples said, “Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?” (Luke 24:32).

Timothy Keller often pointed out that people do not change simply because they are told to. They change when they see Christ as more beautiful and satisfying than the things they have been living for. He liked to cite the Scottish preacher Thomas Chalmers, whose sermon The Expulsive Power of a New Affection argued that the love of the world is driven out not by denouncing it alone, but by a greater love. So application is not only “do this”. It is “look at him, and see why you can”.

Different hearers

Paul described his ministry like this: “Him we proclaim, warning everyone and teaching everyone with all wisdom, that we may present everyone mature in Christ” (Colossians 1:28). Different people need different words: “admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, be patient with them all” (1 Thessalonians 5:14). The Puritans taught preachers to think about the various kinds of people in the room, and apply the same text to each.

A wise preacher pictures them as he prepares. The mature believer needs to be stretched and warned against complacency. The young or doubting Christian needs assurance, to hear that Christ receives the weak. The sufferer needs comfort, not quick answers, and the gentle Saviour of whom it was promised, “a bruised reed he will not break” (Isaiah 42:3). The sceptic needs his objections named fairly and answered honestly. The self-righteous person needs to see that his goodness cannot save him. The careless need a loving but clear warning.

Keller urged preachers to speak as if sceptics were present, even in a room full of believers. Name the objections. Use the words outsiders actually use. Avoid insider jargon, or explain it. Believers benefit too, because they live among sceptics, and their own hearts still doubt.

A man in his thirties came to church only because a friend asked him. He expected to be talked down to. Instead, the preacher paused halfway through and said, “Some of you are thinking this sounds too good to be true, and that is a fair question.” He then took the objection seriously. The man did not believe that day, but he came back the next week, and the week after. The study Apologetics says more about answering such questions.

Commands grounded in grace

Application must be gospel-shaped. The New Testament letters usually explain what God has done before they say what we must do. Romans gives eleven chapters of grace before it says, “I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1). The “therefore” matters. A sermon that piles up commands without the mercies of God crushes people or makes them proud. A sermon that offers mercy without ever calling for change leaves them unchanged. Faithful preaching gives the call, grounded in the gift.

Clarity and plainness

Paul asked for prayer “that I may make it clear” (Colossians 4:4). He warned that unclear speech is useless: “if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle?” (1 Corinthians 14:8). The Puritans prized what they called the “plain style”. William Perkins, in The Art of Prophesying (1592), taught preachers to read the text, explain its sense from Scripture itself, draw out a few profitable points of doctrine from its natural meaning, and apply them in simple, plain speech. Plain does not mean dull. It means that the preacher hides his learning so that the text can shine.

Structure serves clarity. Hearers cannot turn back a page, so a good sermon has a clear main point, a few movements that follow the text, and signposts so people know where they are. Short sentences help. So does repetition of the main idea.

Illustration

Jesus taught in pictures: seeds, coins, sheep, sons, a widow and a judge. Illustrations are windows that let light into an idea. The best come from ordinary life, and the best of all come from Scripture itself. When Nathan told David a story about a rich man who stole a poor man’s lamb, David was furious, until Nathan said, “You are the man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). The story did what a lecture could not. But illustrations must serve the text, not steal attention from it, and a preacher must never use a church member’s story without permission.

Passion and the Spirit

Finally, preaching should be warm. Martyn Lloyd-Jones, in Preaching and Preachers, asked what preaching is, and answered, “Logic on fire! Eloquent reason!” Truth and feeling belong together. A preacher who is moved by what he says is not performing; he is showing that the text is true for him. Yet no preacher can produce real power. Paul’s gospel came “not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction” (1 Thessalonians 1:5). Older writers called this “unction”: the Spirit’s anointing on the preacher and the word. It cannot be manufactured, only prayed for.

For reflection

Which kind of hearer are you most often: the mature, the doubting, the suffering, the sceptical or the careless? Why must commands rest on God’s mercies? Can you remember an illustration that helped you understand a passage? Pray this week for clarity and the Spirit’s power on your church’s preaching.

6.title: Preparing, Hearing and Encouraging Sermons
6.essay:
A sermon is a shared work. The preacher prepares through the week, the congregation prepares to hear, and both depend on the Spirit. This last unit is practical: how a sermon is made, how to listen to one, and how to test and encourage preaching kindly.

Preparing a sermon, step by step

Preachers work in different ways, but most faithful preparation includes these steps.

Pray and read. Begin early in the week. Read the passage many times, in its context, ideally aloud. Ask God to open your eyes and your heart before you open a commentary.

Study the text. Ask what it meant to its first readers. Notice its structure, repeated words, genre and place in the book. Use the original languages if you can, and good commentaries after your own work, not instead of it.

State the point. Write the main point of the passage in one sentence, and then the point for your hearers in another. Most sermons that wander were never clear in the preacher’s own mind.

Trace the line to Christ. Ask how this passage fits the Bible’s story and leads to the gospel, by promise, pattern, theme, contrast or need.

Apply to real people. Picture your congregation: the believer, the doubter, the sufferer, the sceptic. What does this text say to each? What idols does it expose, and what grace does it offer?

Shape and illustrate. Build a simple outline that follows the text. Find a clear introduction that raises the question the passage answers, and a conclusion that brings people to Christ and to a response.

Write, cut and pray again. Leave out much of what you learned. Preach it to yourself first. Then pray for your hearers and go to the pulpit trusting God, not your notes.

How to listen

Jesus said, “Take care then how you hear” (Luke 8:18). Hearing well is a spiritual duty. The Westminster Larger Catechism (Question 160) gives a beautiful summary:

“It is required of those that hear the word preached, that they attend upon it with diligence, preparation, and prayer; examine what they hear by the scriptures; receive the truth with faith, love, meekness, and readiness of mind, as the word of God; meditate, and confer of it; hide it in their hearts, and bring forth the fruit of it in their lives.”

In plain terms: prepare, by going to bed in good time on Saturday, reading the passage beforehand, and praying for the preacher. Listen actively, with your Bible open. Receive the word humbly, as God’s word, not as entertainment to be rated. James puts it this way: “receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls. But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves” (James 1:21–22). Talk about it afterwards, over lunch, with your family or a friend. Do one thing it called you to do.

A father began asking his children at Sunday lunch, “What was the one main thing the sermon said?” At first they shrugged. Within a few months they were listening for it, and so was he. Their conversations about the passage became some of the best family times of the week.

Testing what we hear

Listening humbly does not mean listening uncritically. The Bereans “received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so” (Acts 17:11). Luke calls them “more noble” for it. Paul told the Thessalonians, “test everything; hold fast what is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Every hearer may ask: Was this what the passage says? Was Christ made clear? Was I called to faith and obedience on the basis of grace?

Notice what is not on that list. The test is not whether the preacher was entertaining, whether he agreed with my politics, or whether the sermon was short. Many sermons are imperfect but faithful, and God feeds his people through them. Those who come with eager, prayerful hearts are often fed even by plain preaching, while those who come only to critique find little.

Encouraging kindly

Preachers rarely hear specific encouragement. “Nice sermon, pastor” at the door is kind but tells him little. Tell him instead how the passage helped you, what you understood for the first time, what you are going to do. Paul asks churches “to esteem them very highly in love because of their work” (1 Thessalonians 5:13), and to support them practically: “Let the one who is taught the word share all good things with the one who teaches” (Galatians 6:6).

If you have a real concern, raise it privately, gently and specifically, and with an open Bible, not on the doorstep after the service. Begin by assuming good faith. Elders have a particular duty to help preachers grow, and wise churches build in kind, regular feedback from fellow elders. If preaching is not just weak but false, denying the gospel, or if a leader is domineering or abusive, speak to the other elders, and where there is any abuse, put safety first and report it to the proper authorities. The study The Church says more about elders and accountability.

The word goes on

Sermons end; the word does not. Week by week, through ordinary voices and imperfect preparation, God shapes a people for himself. “Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account. Let them do this with joy and not with groaning” (Hebrews 13:17). A praying, listening, encouraging congregation is one of the greatest gifts a preacher can have, and one of the clearest signs that the word of Christ is dwelling there richly.

For reflection

How could you prepare better to hear God’s word next Sunday? Which part of the Larger Catechism’s summary do you most neglect? What specific encouragement could you give your preacher this week? If you preach, which step of preparation do you most often skip?
